summary:
Malta decriminalised same-sex conduct on 29 January 1973. On 15 April 2014 parliament approved a constitutional amendment naming gender identity as a protected ground, the first European state to do so, and introduced civil unions in the same sitting; same-sex marriage has been legal since 2017. Transgender Europe was among the first non-governmental organisations to welcome gender identity as a protected ground in the highest legal text.

Statutory discrimination protections extend to sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression and sex characteristics, and hate-crime provisions cover sexual-orientation and gender-identity offences. Legal gender recognition requires no surgery, nonbinary identity is recognised, and a December 2016 amendment allows minors aged 16 and over to change their legal gender without a court application or parental approval.

Malta was the first EU country to ban conversion therapy. The Affirmation of Sexual Orientation, Gender Identity and Gender Expression Act passed its final reading unanimously on 6 December 2016, after Civil Liberties Minister Helena Dalli first tabled a bill targeting minors in December 2015; the Malta Chamber of Psychologists and related professional associations backed the measure. The Gender Identity, Gender Expression and Sex Characteristics Act of 2015 was the world's first law to ban sterilising or invasive surgery on intersex infants.

Rules governing everyday access are settled rather than contested: same-sex marriage since 2017, full joint adoption since 2014, open military service, protected bathroom access, a ban on conversion therapy, and a full ban on intersex infant surgery. The age of consent is 16 regardless of sexual orientation or gender.

Border treatment of LGBTI arrivals is documented in one live litigation. An LGBTI asylum seeker was detained on arrival in Malta in April 2023 and received a return decision and removal order to Bangladesh in May 2024. On 30 July 2025 the International Commission of Jurists and partner organisations filed observations in M.S. v. Malta at the European Court of Human Rights, raising non-refoulement, detention conditions and the requirement of an individualised assessment before detention under Articles 3, 5 and 13 of the European Convention on Human Rights.

Violence indicators are comparatively favourable but reporting is not. Malta records one of the lowest rates of physical and sexual victimisation on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity expression in the EU27, while LGBTIQ+ people still report a comparatively high share of harassment and online hatred, and reporting of violence to the Malta Police Force remains significantly low despite institutional reforms.

Prison is the documented weak point. On 29 May 2018 the Maltese civil court (Judge Silvio Meli) awarded seven transgender inmates of Corradino prison €5,000 each — €4,000 for breach of rights and €1,000 for damage to personal dignity — after the authorities held them in the male section, where they shared cells with male inmates, used the men's showers and often went without washing, and endured insults and continuous sexual abuse and violence. The court found that the authorities had knowingly and repeatedly placed them in situations of high risk of sexual and psychological violence; the only alternative offered, transfer to the female section, would have cost them the work and study opportunities they needed to pay for hormone therapy, and female inmates and warders were described as hostile, so they remained in the male section. The director of prisons was ordered to pay, and the Aditus Foundation represented the seven women.

Practice in custody continues to lag the statute. A 2024 University of Malta dissertation by Oriana Vidal, drawing on interviews with four current and former transgender and gender-diverse inmates of the Correctional Service Agency across a 25-year cohort, records that after the 2013 gender-law reform the Agency permitted transfers to the female section, replacing an earlier practice of segregating such inmates in a separate dormitory. Participants now hold individual cells in the female section but report residual misgendering by officers using masculine birth names, along with gaps in gender-appropriate clothing and healthcare, and conclude that Agency practice, policies and procedures lag the national gender-identity law. The dissertation also identifies gaps in healthcare, legislation and staff knowledge, and problems after release.
tangentialFactors:
ILGA-Europe's Rainbow Map scores Malta's national compliance category by category across asylum, civil-society space, intersex bodily integrity, legal gender recognition, hate crime and hate speech, and equality body, on the map's red-to-green scale; the map is a comparative instrument rather than a statement of Maltese law, and a high score does not describe conditions in any individual case.

Public attitudes and workplace climate diverge. Equaldex data records 84% rating Malta a 'good place' for gay people, while Maltese respondents rank first of 30 EU regions for hiding being LGBTIQ at work — concealment on the job sits alongside a strong statutory framework and may shape what a visitor reads off day-to-day interactions.

Comparative victimisation figures cut both ways: Malta's low rate of physical and sexual victimisation in the EU27 sits beside elevated reported harassment and online hatred and a persistently low rate of reporting to the police, so official incident counts understate what LGBTIQ+ people describe.
localsOnly:
Education policy has been contested domestically. MGRM's petition to Parliament in February 2008 demanded an anti-homophobic bullying strategy for Maltese schools. In 2015 Education Minister Evarist Bartolo refused to distribute reading material donated by MGRM that taught diverse families including same-sex parenting. In June 2021 Malta opposed, at an EU conference, any law prohibiting the teaching and distribution of LGBT information to children.

Workplace disclosure is a resident-facing issue: Maltese respondents rank first among 30 EU regions for hiding being LGBTIQ at work, despite discrimination being illegal across sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression and sex characteristics.

Corrections practice for transgender and gender-diverse inmates is governed by the Correctional Service Agency, whose procedures are described by interviewed inmates as behind the national gender-identity legislation on clothing, healthcare and naming; post-release support is also identified as deficient.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the 2018 Corradino award changed Correctional Service Agency practice is not sourced here. The 2024 dissertation reports ongoing misgendering and clothing and healthcare gaps, but the inventory contains no post-judgment inspection, no agency policy revision, and no compliance review tied to the ruling.

The dissertation rests on four interviews across a 25-year cohort at one corrections agency, and the underlying 2018 award covers seven claimants. Both are specific findings rather than a count of current conditions in custody.

M.S. v. Malta was still at the observation stage as of 30 July 2025; the inventory contains no judgment of the European Court of Human Rights, so the outcome of the claim and any resulting change in detention practice at the border remain unresolved.

Police reporting rates are described only as 'significantly low' in the academic source. The inventory carries no figure for complaints of hate-motivated violence, no prosecutorial outcomes, and no data disaggregating incidents against transgender people specifically.

Equaldex's public-attitude percentage and workplace-concealment ranking are platform and survey data of unstated methodology; the inventory does not establish their sampling, date or comparability with the ILGA-Europe scoring.
